correctness.rationale: Three unit complex numbers summing to zero must form the equilateral triple, so a Fourier zero has one of two oriented phase targets. The homomorphism from frequency to the two support characters has kernel size \(g\), making each nonempty orientation fiber size \(g\). The second orientation occurs iff their ratio \((\rho,\rho^2)\) lies in the homomorphism image. Reducing the resulting congruences modulo the primitive order gives exactly the stated divisibility-by-three and complete-residue criterion. A zero-free phase pair exists because only finitely many phase-torus points are forbidden. An independent brute arithmetic replay through \(N=60\) found no discrepancy between the residue criterion and direct image membership.
correctness.risk: The theorem is phase-specific and exactly three-sparse; approximate cancellation is outside scope.

final_claim: For a three-point equal-magnitude signal on \(\mathbb Z_N\), let \(g\) be the common gcd of \(N\) and the two support differences and \(n=N/g\). Every nonempty Fourier zero set has exactly \(2g\) zeros precisely when \(3\mid n\) and the primitive support occupies all three residue classes modulo three; otherwise it has exactly \(g\) zero. Zero-free phases also exist. Hence for prime \(p>3\), at most one Fourier zero is possible and one is attainable.
limitations: Exactly three support points and equal nonzero coefficient magnitudes.
No noncyclic finite Abelian extension or perturbative stability statement.
